overview: A retaining wall has one job: hold back dirt that wants to move. Done right, it turns a slope into flat, usable yard, stops erosion and keeps water off the foundation. Done wrong, it leans, bows and cracks within a few seasons. The difference is almost always in the parts you can't see.

Every wall we build starts the same way. We dig below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level, because every row above inherits what that bottom row does. Behind the wall goes gravel backfill and a perforated drain tied out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. Taller walls get geogrid tied back into the hill and a slight lean into the slope. We build with segmental block from brands like Belgard and Pavestone, natural stone, boulders and pressure-treated timber.

process.title: Read the slope
process.text: We walk the site, measure the grade change, find where the water comes from, and figure out what the wall has to hold.

process.title: Spec and price the wall
process.text: You get a written, itemized estimate with the material, height, length and drainage. If the wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough.

process.title: Dig and set the base
process.text: We excavate below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level.

process.title: Build it up with drainage
process.text: Each course goes up with gravel backfill behind it, a perforated drain at the bottom, and geogrid on taller walls.

process.title: Finish and grade
process.text: We finish the top of the wall, grade the ground above and below it so water moves off, and haul away the spoil.

timing: We build walls year-round. A dry stretch is the best time to dig and compact, since wet clay won't pack down right. If a slope is already washing out or a wall is starting to lean, don't wait for the spring rains to make it worse.

east_texas.title: Why walls fail here, and how we stop it
text: Most failed walls in our area come down to water. East Texas clay swells when it's wet and shrinks when it dries, and behind a wall that water has nowhere to go. It builds pressure against the block until the wall leans, then bows, then cracks. We put a gravel chimney and a perforated drain behind every wall so that pressure never builds.

The second weak spot is the base. Sandy loam over clay won't hold a wall set on undisturbed dirt. At Lake Cherokee, we took a leaning block wall along a driveway and rebuilt it course by course on a compacted base, with drainage fabric and pipe behind it. A real base and somewhere for the water to go fixes most walls.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Longview, TX?
faq.a: Most walls we build run $3,000 to $19,000, and height and length move the number most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars. A tall structural wall with geogrid and drainage runs $20,000 or more. The material and how much digging the slope needs matter too. We walk the site and send a written, itemized estimate before any dirt moves.

faq.q: What is the best retaining wall material for East Texas?
faq.a: For most yards, segmental block from brands like Belgard and Pavestone. It locks together, flexes with the ground and goes up clean. Natural stone and boulder walls cost more but look great on the right property. Pressure-treated timber fits some jobs, like the timber wall we built for a raised boat and RV pad in White Oak.

Yes, and in East Texas clay it's the most important part of the build. Water that collects behind a wall builds pressure and pushes it out over time. Every wall we build gets gravel backfill and a perforated drain that carries water to daylight or a pop-up emitter, so that pressure never gets a chance to build.

faq.q: How tall can a retaining wall be?
faq.a: We build everything from short garden and seating walls to tall structural walls. Walls over about four feet usually need engineered design and reinforcement like geogrid, and we handle the base prep, grid and drainage that taller walls require. If your wall calls for a stamped engineering plan, we'll tell you during the walkthrough.

faq.q: Can a leaning retaining wall be fixed?
faq.a: Propping it up won't hold. A leaning wall almost always has a base or drainage problem, and the real fix is taking it down and building it back right. At Lake Cherokee we rebuilt a leaning block wall along a driveway course by course on a compacted base, with drainage fabric and pipe behind it. We'll tell you at the walkthrough what yours needs.
